resources.string: Android, or Play Protect, may ask once more. That is their own check and not a problem with the file.
This device always asks before an update is installed.
Every Android app has one name that never changes. A file that carried another name would be a different app, whatever it called itself.

A developer signs every release with a key only they hold. Tern compares the signature of this file with the app on this device and with the certificate it remembered at the first install. A file signed by anyone else is refused, even if it comes from the right address.
There is nothing to compare with yet. The file says who signed it, Android confirms that when it installs, and from then on Tern holds every update to the same certificate.
A checksum is a fingerprint of the file itself. The publisher gave one, and the file Tern downloaded has the same, so it arrived as it was published.
A checksum is a fingerprint of the file itself. The publisher gave one, and Tern compares it with the file as soon as the file is downloaded.
A checksum is a fingerprint of the file itself. The publisher gave one, and the file Tern downloaded has another, so it is not the file that was published.
This publisher gives no checksum. The signature is still checked, and it is the stronger of the two.
What this version asks to be allowed to do that the installed one did not.
Opens the page for this exact file at VirusTotal in your browser. Tern sends nothing there.
Android lets an app update another without asking when that app installed it and the device runs Android 12 or later. Android decides each time.
This device runs Android %1$s, which asks before every install. Tern downloads and checks the update in the background and tells you when it is ready.
